cards.text: Dresden is the capital of Saxony, right on the river Elbe. About 570,000 people live here, and its baroque old town earned it the nickname Florence on the Elbe.
Dresden has about 570,000 people. In Saxony only Leipzig is a little bigger.
Dresden was first mentioned in a document in 1206, so the city celebrated its 800th birthday in 2006.
People call Dresden Florence on the Elbe, because of its baroque churches, palaces and art treasures along the river.
The name Dresden comes from an old Sorbian word for people living in the riverside forest or marshland.
The Frauenkirche is Dresden's famous baroque Lutheran church with a huge stone dome. It was built from 1726 to 1743, destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt by 2005.
The Frauenkirche was first built from 1726 to 1743, to a design by George Bähr. It was destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt by 2005.
The Frauenkirche is about 91 metres tall, crowned by a golden cross on top of its big stone dome.
The Frauenkirche was rebuilt from 1994 and consecrated again in 2005. The dark stones you see are original ones, rescued from the ruins.
The Frauenkirche collapsed two days after the bombing in February 1945. For almost fifty years its pile of stones stayed in the square as a memorial against war.
The golden cross on the Frauenkirche was a gift from Britain. It was made by a London goldsmith whose father had flown in the 1945 bombing raids.
The Frauenkirche was designed by George Bähr, the city's master carpenter. Its stone dome is nicknamed the stone bell.
The Neumarkt is the square around the Frauenkirche, lined with rebuilt baroque houses. Martin Luther's statue stands right in front of the church.
The Zwinger is a baroque palace with pavilions, fountains and a big courtyard, built from 1710 to 1728 for Augustus the Strong by architect Pöppelmann.
Inside the Zwinger you'll find the Old Masters Picture Gallery, a huge porcelain collection and a salon full of old clocks and science instruments.
The Zwinger's Crown Gate wears a golden crown on top, and its hidden Nymph Bath is a little grotto of fountains and stone nymphs.
The Old Masters Picture Gallery in the Zwinger holds paintings by Raphael, Rembrandt, Vermeer and Canaletto. It's one of the great art collections of Europe.
Raphael's Sistine Madonna hangs in the Old Masters gallery. The two bored little angels at the bottom are famous all over the world.
Vermeer's Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window hangs in Dresden's Old Masters gallery. A hidden Cupid painting on its wall was uncovered in a restoration.
Bernardo Bellotto, called Canaletto, painted Dresden from across the Elbe in the 1700s. From the Neustadt bank you can still see almost the same view.
The Semperoper is Dresden's opera house, named after architect Gottfried Semper. It was destroyed in 1945 and reopened in 1985, exactly forty years after the bombing.
The Staatskapelle Dresden plays at the Semperoper. It was founded in 1548, which makes it one of the oldest orchestras in the world.
Theaterplatz is the big square between the Semperoper, the Zwinger, the palace and the Court Church. It's one of the prettiest spots in town.
The Residenzschloss was home to Saxony's electors and kings. Today it holds the Green Vault treasures, the armoury and the Turkish Chamber.
The Turkish Chamber in the palace shows Ottoman treasures, including a giant three-masted silk tent. Saxon rulers loved collecting them.
The Green Vault is Augustus the Strong's treasure chamber in the palace, full of gold, jewels, ivory and amber. It's one of the richest treasuries in Europe.
The Dresden Green is a rare natural green diamond of about 41 carats, kept with the Green Vault treasures.
In November 2019 thieves broke into the Green Vault and stole jewels. Most of the pieces were found and returned a few years later.
The Fürstenzug is a 102 metre long mural of Saxony's rulers on horseback, made from about 23,000 Meissen porcelain tiles. It survived the 1945 bombing.
The Hofkirche, or Court Church, is Dresden's Catholic cathedral, finished in 1755. Augustus the Strong's heart is kept in its crypt.
Legend says Augustus the Strong's heart, kept in the Hofkirche crypt, starts to beat when a pretty woman walks by.
Augustus the Strong was Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, living from 1670 to 1733. He built much of baroque Dresden and loved art and porcelain.
The Golden Rider is a shiny gilded statue of Augustus the Strong on horseback, at the Neustadt end of the Augustus Bridge, from the 1730s.
The Brühl Terrace is a long promenade high above the Elbe, nicknamed the Balcony of Europe. It's lovely for a sunset walk.
The ribbed glass dome of the Art Academy on the Brühl Terrace is nicknamed the lemon squeezer. It really does look like one!
The Albertinum shows art from the Romantics to today, including many works by Gerhard Richter, who was born in Dresden in 1932.
The Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich lived and worked in Dresden for most of his life. You can see his moody landscapes in the Albertinum.
The Kreuzkirche on the Altmarkt is Dresden's main Protestant church and the home of the famous Kreuzchor boys' choir.
The Dresdner Kreuzchor is a boys' choir with more than 800 years of history. Its singers perform at the Kreuzkirche and travel the world.
The Altmarkt is Dresden's old market square. The Striezelmarkt is held here at Christmas, and next to it the Kulturpalast is home to the Dresden Philharmonic.
The Striezelmarkt is one of Germany's oldest Christmas markets, first held in 1434. It's named after Striezel, the old word for Stollen.
Dresdner Stollen is a buttery Christmas fruit bread dusted with sugar. Every December a giant Stollen is paraded through town and cut with a huge knife.
Eierschecke is a Saxon cake with three layers: a yeast base, a quark filling and a fluffy egg custard on top. Yummy!
The Yenidze looks like a mosque but was built in 1909 as a cigarette factory. Its colourful glass dome now has a restaurant with fairy-tale readings.
The Elbe flows through Dresden on its way from the Czech mountains to the North Sea, about 1,100 kilometres in all.
Dresden keeps wide green meadows along the Elbe, so the river has room when it floods. In summer there's open-air cinema on the riverbank.
In August 2002 the Elbe rose to 9.40 metres in Dresden, its highest level on record. The water reached the Zwinger and the main station.
The Dresden Elbe Valley was a UNESCO World Heritage Site from 2004, but lost the title in 2009 because of the new Waldschlösschen Bridge.
The Waldschlösschen Bridge opened in 2013 across the Elbe meadows. Building it cost Dresden its UNESCO World Heritage title.
The Augustus Bridge links the old town with the Neustadt. A bridge has stood here since the Middle Ages; today's stone one dates from 1910.
The Blue Wonder is a blue steel bridge from 1893 between Blasewitz and Loschwitz. Locals saved it from being blown up at the end of the war.
Loschwitz has two hill railways: a funicular from 1895 and a hanging suspension railway from 1901, one of the oldest of its kind in the world.
Dresden has one of the oldest and largest fleets of historic paddle steamers in the world. They cruise the Elbe up to Saxon Switzerland.
The Äußere Neustadt is Dresden's lively, alternative quarter, full of street art, cafés, bars and little shops. It's the place to go out at night.
Every June the Neustadt throws the Bunte Republik Neustadt, a big street festival with music on every corner.
The Kunsthofpassage is a string of colourful courtyards in the Neustadt. In the Courtyard of the Elements, the drainpipes on the wall play music when it rains.
Pfunds Molkerei is a dairy shop from 1880 covered in hand-painted tiles. It's often called the most beautiful dairy shop in the world.
The Großer Garten is Dresden's big baroque park, with a summer palace in the middle, a lake, boat rides and a little park railway.
The little railway in the Großer Garten is run mostly by children and teenagers, who work as conductors and station staff.
Zoo Dresden sits at the edge of the Großer Garten. It opened in 1861, making it one of the oldest zoos in Germany.
The Transparent Factory by the Großer Garten is a glass car factory by Volkswagen, opened in 2002. Today it shows off electric cars.
The German Hygiene Museum is a fun museum about the human body. Its famous Glass Man, a see-through human figure, was first shown in 1930.
Karl August Lingner made his fortune with Odol mouthwash and founded the Hygiene Museum in 1912. His villa above the Elbe is called Lingnerschloss.
The Military History Museum is an old arsenal sliced by a giant steel and glass wedge designed by Daniel Libeskind. It opened in 2011.
The Panometer is an old gas tank that shows huge 360 degree panorama pictures by Yadegar Asisi, for example baroque Dresden or the city in 1945.
Dresden Hauptbahnhof is the main train station. Its old halls got a bright new roof of glass-fibre membrane designed by Norman Foster.
Dresden's yellow trams and buses are run by the DVB. There are about a dozen tram lines, and they're the easiest way to get around town.
You can buy tram tickets at the machines at stops or on the trams, or in the DVB app. Paper tickets need to be stamped when you board.
The S-Bahn trains connect Dresden with Meissen, Pirna and Saxon Switzerland. The S1 runs along the Elbe all the way to Bad Schandau.
Prague is only a little over two hours away by train, along the Elbe valley. Dresden is very close to the Czech border.
Berlin is about two hours from Dresden by train, and a little less by car on a good day.
Dresden Airport is in Klotzsche, north of the city. The S-Bahn S2 takes you there from the main station.
On 13 to 15 February 1945, British and American air raids caused a firestorm that destroyed the old town. About 25,000 people were killed.
Every 13 February, Dresden remembers the bombing. Thousands of people hold hands in a human chain around the old town, and the church bells ring.
After the war Dresden was part of East Germany, the GDR, until Germany reunited in 1990.
In East German times Dresden was jokingly called the Valley of the Clueless, because West German TV signals couldn't reach it.
In autumn 1989 thousands of people in Dresden marched peacefully for freedom. A month later the Berlin Wall fell.
Saxony is a German state of about four million people. Dresden is its capital, Leipzig its biggest city, and it borders Poland and the Czech Republic.
Saxons speak a soft, sing-song dialect called Sächsisch. Locals might say Ei verbibbsch, which means something like oh my goodness.
Dresden is Europe's biggest microelectronics hub, nicknamed Silicon Saxony. Big chip factories here make semiconductors for cars and phones.
Meissen, just down the Elbe, made Europe's first true porcelain in 1710. Its crossed blue swords mark is famous worldwide.
Pillnitz Palace is a summer palace on the Elbe with Chinese-style roofs. Its gardens have a camellia over 200 years old that gets its own glasshouse in winter.
Moritzburg Castle is a yellow baroque hunting lodge on a lake north of Dresden. It's where the film Three Hazelnuts for Cinderella was shot.
Saxon Switzerland is a national park of sandstone cliffs along the Elbe, under an hour away by S-Bahn. It's perfect for a day of hiking.
The Bastei is a famous lookout high above the Elbe in Saxon Switzerland, with a stone bridge from 1851 running between the rock towers.
Königstein Fortress sits on a huge flat-topped rock above the Elbe. It's one of the largest hilltop fortresses in Europe.
Karl May, who wrote the Winnetou adventure stories, lived in Radebeul right next to Dresden. His villa is now the Karl May Museum.
The Elbe slopes around Dresden and Radebeul grow wine. It's one of the most northerly wine regions in Europe.
The Dresdner Heide is a big forest on the city's north side, great for walks and bike rides.
The Elbe Cycle Route runs right through Dresden along the river. It's one of Germany's most popular bike routes.
Dynamo Dresden is the city's football club. Its fans in black and yellow are famous for their loud songs in the stadium.
TU Dresden is one of Germany's biggest technical universities, with about 30,000 students. It was founded in 1828 and is a University of Excellence.
